questions.q: Match the characteristics with the names.
items: When the abbreviation for this phase is (s), the substance is:
When the abbreviation for this phase is (aq), the substance is:
When something dissolves in a specific solvent (water in this course) it is:
When a precipitate forms, it is a product that is:
If a substance dissociates in water, it is:
When something splits apart into positive and negative ions when it is added to a solvent it is said to be:
When something does not dissolve and instead either falls into a pile of solid at the bottom of the container or disperses into tiny solid pieces making the liquid look cloudy, it is:
questions.note: (s) = solid = insoluble. (aq) = dissolved = soluble. A precipitate is a solid, so it is insoluble.

questions.q: Mark all reactions which are NOT expected to be successful as written. (These are the reactions that will have "no reaction" for their net ionic equation.) Notice that all states/phases are already given for each compound.
questions.note: Look only at the product phases. All (aq) → no reaction. A solid (s), gas (g) or liquid water (l) means it goes.

questions.q: Identify the full ionic equation for aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous nickel(II) acetate producing aqueous sodium acetate and solid nickel(II) hydroxide.
opts: 2 Na⁺ (aq) + 2 OH⁻ (aq) + Ni²⁺ (aq) + 2 C₂H₃O₂⁻ (aq) → Ni(OH)₂ (s) + 2 Na⁺ (aq) + 2 C₂H₃O₂⁻ (aq)
2 Na⁺ (aq) + 2 OH⁻ (aq) + Ni²⁺ (aq) + 2 C₂H₃O₂⁻ (aq) → Ni²⁺ (aq) + 2 OH⁻ (aq) + 2 NaC₂H₃O₂ (s)
questions.given: (Not related to this problem, but can you also identify whether the reaction will proceed, the net equation, and the spectator ions?)
questions.note: Full ionic: every (aq) split into ions, the solid Ni(OH)₂ kept together. Net: 2 OH⁻ + Ni²⁺ → Ni(OH)₂. Spectators: Na⁺ and C₂H₃O₂⁻.

questions.q: Which of the following is the full ionic equation for the balanced reaction between aqueous lead(II) nitrate and aqueous potassium iodide that produces solid lead(II) iodide and aqueous potassium nitrate?
questions.note: The first choice is the net ionic equation; the full ionic keeps the spectators K⁺ and NO₃⁻.

questions.q: Which of the following is the net ionic equation for the balanced reaction between aqueous ammonium iodide and aqueous mercury(I) nitrate that produces solid mercury(I) iodide and aqueous ammonium nitrate?
questions.given: NOTE: The symbol for mercury(I) nitrate is unusual. It is Hg₂(NO₃)₂, and when dissolved in water it becomes Hg₂²⁺ and 2NO₃⁻. The symbol for solid mercury(I) iodide is Hg₂I₂.
questions.note: Cancel the spectators (NH₄⁺ and NO₃⁻); what is left is the ions that make the solid.

questions.q: Which reaction will not proceed?
opts: two aqueous reactants producing two aqueous products
two aqueous reactants producing aqueous product(s) and water
two aqueous reactants producing aqueous product(s) and a gas
two aqueous reactants producing aqueous product(s) and a solid
questions.note: A solid, a gas or water drives a reaction. All (aq) → no reaction.

questions.q: What are the oxidation numbers for each element in: N₂O
questions.note: O gets its charge, −2. Neutral: 2N − 2 = 0, so N = +1.

questions.q: What are the oxidation numbers for each element in: NCl₃
questions.note: Cl is more electronegative and gets its charge, −1. N + 3(−1) = 0, so N = +3.

questions.q: What are the oxidation numbers for each element in: BrO₃⁻
questions.note: O = −2. The ion totals −1: Br + 3(−2) = −1, so Br = +5.

questions.q: What are the oxidation numbers for each element in: Na₂C₂O₄
This question is different from the ones above it. What are the oxidation numbers for each element or ion in the list below?
questions.note: Any neutral element (even diatomic) is 0. An ion's oxidation number is its charge.

questions.q: Use these reactions. Rxn 1: Fe → Fe³⁺ + 3e⁻. Rxn 2: O₂ + 4e⁻ → 2O²⁻.

blanks.label: Which reaction is an oxidation? (type Rxn 1 or Rxn 2)
Symbol of the element that is the oxidizing agent
Symbol of the element that is the reducing agent

questions.note: Electrons on the right = lost = oxidation (Fe, the reducing agent). Electrons on the left = gained = reduction (O, the oxidizing agent).

questions.q: Use these reactions. Rxn 1: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Rxn 2: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻.

blanks.label: Which reaction is an oxidation? (type Rxn 1 or Rxn 2)
Symbol of the oxidizing agent (include its charge if it has one)
Look at these on the activity series. Will these two reactions occur spontaneously together? (yes/no)

questions.note: Cu²⁺ gains electrons, so it is the oxidizing agent. Fe is above Cu on the activity series, so neutral Fe can give its electrons to Cu²⁺: yes.

questions.q: Use the activity series to determine if a reaction will proceed. Select all correct answers.
questions.note: The neutral metal must be higher on the activity series than the ion's metal. Zn is above Cu and H; Ag is below Cu; Hg is below Co.

questions.q: Match the choices about oxidation/reduction with their answers.
items: Has the electrons listed on the right side of the arrow
These are examples that still need electrons added: O₂⁰ → O⁻², N⁻³ → N⁻¹, Mn⁵⁺ → Mn³⁺
These are examples that still need electrons added: Zn⁰ → Zn⁺², Fe²⁺ → Fe⁴⁺, 2F⁻ → F₂⁰
The reactant is the oxidizing agent
The reactant is the reducing agent
Has the electrons listed on the left side of the arrow
questions.note: Charge going down = gaining electrons = reduction; going up = losing = oxidation. Heads-up: N⁻³ → N⁻¹ goes up, so it is really an oxidation, but the homework counts that first group as reduction.

questions.q: To use the activity series, compare the two reactants. If the reactant that is neutral is higher than the reactant that has a charge, the reaction will proceed.
